criterion_notes.c1: Fails Criterion 1: The paper examines general municipal efficiency across South African local governments rather than household or community water or sanitation service access. Water supply and sanitation are mentioned only in passing in a single two-sentence paragraph on eThekwini Municipality alongside waste management and public transport in Cape Town, with no investigation of water or sanitation access.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper passes (plain=yes) because it examines political, administrative, and fiscal decentralization in local governance. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, the paper fails (narrow=no) because it measures only a broad macro-governance perception score of general municipal decentralization rather than any specific rule-type mechanism directly governing water or sanitation service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure rules, tariff or cost-recovery rules, discretion, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure). Note that even under the plain reading of Criterion 2, the study is still excluded because it fails Criteria 1, 4, and 5.
criterion_notes.c3: Satisfies Criterion 3 minimally by reporting descriptive statistics and multiple regression results from a structured survey of local government personnel plus brief qualitative case summaries, although methodological reporting is severely incomplete (sample sizes and instruments are omitted).
criterion_notes.c4: Fails Criterion 4: Quantitative outcomes are local officials' perceptions of overall resource management efficiency, generic municipal service delivery quality, and general public satisfaction; no household or community water or sanitation access, connection, continuity, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion outcome is measured.
criterion_notes.c5: Fails Criterion 5: While a cross-sectional mixed-methods design is stated, the paper never reports sample sizes (number of surveyed personnel, municipalities, or interviewees) and provides no identifiable water/sanitation exposure or access outcome operationalization.

evidence_quotes.quote: This study evaluates the impact of decentralization on the efficiency of local governments in South Africa. By examining both quantitative and qualitative data, the research explores how decentralization influences resource management, service delivery, and public satisfaction.

The primary numeric technique involves structured surveys of local government personnel across numerous South African municipalities. These surveys inquire about decentralisation, resource management, service quality, and public satisfaction.
The average scores for perceived decentralization (M = 3.85), resource management efficiency (M = 3.45), service delivery quality (M = 3.75), and public satisfaction (M = 3.60) are not very high.

Decentralisation has improved community coordination in eThekwini municipality. This has enhanced sanitation and water supply in regions like local authorities empowered by the dispersed approach, which may make service quality choices, thereby boosting public trust and satisfaction.

raw_response.exposure: Perceived level of local government decentralization (general political, administrative, and fiscal decentralization)
raw_response.outcome: Perceived municipal resource management efficiency, generic service delivery quality, and overall public satisfaction
raw_response.population_and_sample: Local government personnel across South African municipalities and city officials, council members, and community leaders in Cape Town and eThekwini Municipality (sample sizes not reported)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic): this public administration study evaluates generic municipal decentralization and overall local government efficiency (resource management efficiency, aggregate service delivery quality, and general public satisfaction) as perceived by municipal officials. It does not study household or community water or sanitation service access (mentioning water supply and sanitation only in passing in a two-sentence summary of eThekwini), does not examine a rule-type mechanism governing water or sanitation access under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification, reports no water/sanitation access outcomes, and omits all sample sizes. It would also be excluded under the plain wording of Criterion 2 due to failing Criteria 1, 4, and 5.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional mixed-methods study (structured survey of local government personnel with multiple regression analysis and brief qualitative case summaries)
